 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The PDF is the original article 'The Effects of On-Field Heat Index and Altitude on Concussion Assessments and Recovery Among NCAA Athletes' (Sports Medicine, article DOI 10.1007/s40279-020-01395-5 printed on page 1), which matches the filename; the batch externalDoi 10.1007/s40279-020-01425-2 is the Crossref record for the 'Correction to:' notice, so it was not used and this needs operator confirmation.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Collegiate", "Injured Athletes", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective cohort of 187 collegiate athletes (71% male; 44% football and 34% soccer) with a concussion during outdoor competition, drawn from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium between 2014 and 2018. Altitude at the injury site did not predict any acute assessment or recovery outcome (p of 0.265 or higher), while higher heat index was associated with fewer days to symptom recovery (estimate -0.1 days per degree, p = 0.047, R2 = 0.06) and clinical recovery (-0.3 days per degree, p = 0.006, R2 = 0.09). Heat index did not predict SCAT, BESS or ImPACT scores within 48 hours (p of 0.200 or higher).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Core temperature was not measured, so heat index is only a proxy for thermal stress, and travel, acclimatization and season timing were not controlled. Almost all injuries occurred below 500 m and no athlete was at true high altitude (2,500 m or more), and sample sizes for some acute measures fell to 86 to 121.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the heat index result as a sign that hot conditions shorten recovery or should change return-to-play timing, when the authors describe the effects as small (R2 of 0.06 to 0.09) and probably not clinically meaningful.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Lempke LB, Lynall RC, Le RK, McCrea M, McAllister T, Schmidt JD, et al. The Effects of On-Field Heat Index and Altitude on Concussion Assessments and Recovery Among NCAA Athletes. Sports Medicine. 2020.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s40279-020-01395-5",
   "abstract": "In 187 NCAA athletes concussed during competition, on-field altitude did not predict any acute assessment or recovery outcome. Higher heat index at the time of injury was associated with slightly shorter symptom and clinical recovery, and the authors describe these effects as small and probably not clinically meaningful.",
   "tldr": "Altitude at the time of concussion (below 2,500 m) did not affect acute tests or recovery in collegiate athletes. Hotter conditions at injury were linked to a small reduction in recovery time, which the authors judge unlikely to be clinically meaningful.",
   "methods": "Retrospective cohort from the CARE Consortium (2014 to 2018) of athletes with a first concussion during outdoor, in-season competition who had baseline and post-injury assessments. Air temperature and humidity were taken from Weather Underground and converted to heat index, and altitude came from Google Earth Pro. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for age, sex and concussion history, tested heat index and altitude against SCAT, BESS and ImPACT changes within 48 hours and against days to symptom and clinical recovery.",
   "findings": "Altitude (median 181 m, range -0.6 to 2,202 m) did not predict any outcome (p of 0.265 or higher). Heat index (median 17.8 C) was associated with fewer days to symptom recovery (estimate -0.1, p = 0.047, R2 = 0.06) and clinical recovery (estimate -0.3, p = 0.006, R2 = 0.09), with sex and concussion history also significant for recovery. Heat index did not predict acute SCAT, BESS or ImPACT scores (p of 0.200 or higher). In post-hoc models, heat index was not significant for home games, and for away games it was significant only for clinical recovery (p = 0.006).",
   "limitations": "Core temperature was not measured, so heat index was used as a proxy, and the authors did not control for acclimatization, travel or season timing. The heat index effect is reported inconsistently: the abstract and discussion give 0.05 and 0.14 days, the Results text gives 0.22 days for clinical recovery and 7.12 days for male sex, and Table 3 gives -0.1 and -0.3 (male sex -3.7 days); this summary uses the Table 3 values. Samples for some acute measures fell below 100, and the study did not include true high-altitude injuries. The printed year is 2020 (copyright), while Crossref lists 2021 for a correction notice on this article.",
   "practicalImplications": "Altitude at the time of concussion below 2,500 m does not need to be considered when assessing an athlete or planning recovery. Hotter conditions at injury were linked to slightly faster recovery, not worse outcomes, but the authors judge this not clinically meaningful, so it should not change return-to-play decisions. Heat index was used as a proxy, so this does not show how core temperature affects concussion recovery.",
   "athleteDev": "The findings give performance staff no basis to change post-concussion training around altitude or heat, since the study did not measure training load, acclimatization or core temperature. Its data cover only concussion recovery timelines.",
   "rtp": "Altitude at injury had no association with days to symptom or clinical recovery, so it should not be used to plan return to play. The small heat index association is not clinically meaningful according to the authors, so it cannot set return-to-play timing. The study does not test return-to-play criteria and cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to play."
 }
}

17	Abstract
18	Background Recent literature has indicated altitude may be a protective factor for concussion but it is unknown whether
19	altitude or heat index affects recovery.
20	Objective To examine whether on-field heat index and altitude at the time of injury alter acute (< 48 h) concussion assess-
21	ments, days-to-asymptomatic, and days-to-return-to-play in collegiate athletes following concussion.
22	Methods Collegiate athletes (n = 187; age = 19.7 ± 1.4 years; male = 70.6%) underwent baseline assessments across 30
23	universities and experienced a concussion in this retrospective cohort study. Altitude (m) and heat index (°C) at the time
24	and location of injury were determined using valid online database tools. Acute concussion assessments included the Sport
25	Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) symptom inventory, Balance Error Scoring System (BESS), and the Immediate Post-
26	Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT). We used multiple linear regression models to determine whether
27	heat index and altitude predicted each acute assessment outcome, days-to-asymptomatic, and days-to-return-to-play.
28	Results Collegiate athletes were concussed at a 181.1 m (range − 0.6 to 2201.9 m) median altitude and 17.8 °C (range − 6.1
29	to 35.6 °C) median heat index. Altitude did not predict (p ≥ 0.265) any outcomes. Every one-degree increase in heat index
30	reduced days-to-asymptomatic (p = 0.047; R2 = 0.06) and days-to-return-to-play (p = 0.006; R2 = 0.09) by 0.05 and 0.14 days,
31	respectively. Heat index and altitude did not explain significant variance in SCAT, BESS, and ImPACT composite scores
32	(p’s = 0.20–0.922).
33	Conclusion Our findings suggest that on-field altitude and heat index at the time of injury do not contribute to clinically
34	meaningful changes on acute assessments or concussion recovery. On-field altitude and heat index do not appear to signifi-
35	cantly alter assessment outcomes or clinical recovery, suggesting that environmental factors at altitudes below < 2500 m are
36	negligible outcomes for researchers and clinicians to consider post-concussion.

The Effects of On‑Field Heat Index and Altitude on Concussion
Assessments and Recovery Among NCAA Athletes
Landon B. Lempke1 · Robert C. Lynall1 · Rachel K. Le1 · Michael McCrea2,3 · Thomas McAllister4 ·
Julianne D. Schmidt1 · CARE Consortium Investigators

Accepted: 21 November 2020
© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2020


Abstract
Background Recent literature has indicated altitude may be a protective factor for concussion but it is unknown whether
altitude or heat index affects recovery.
Objective To examine whether on-field heat index and altitude at the time of injury alter acute (< 48 h) concussion assess-
ments, days-to-asymptomatic, and days-to-return-to-play in collegiate athletes following concussion.
Methods Collegiate athletes (n = 187; age = 19.7 ± 1.4 years; male = 70.6%) underwent baseline assessments across 30
universities and experienced a concussion in this retrospective cohort study. Altitude (m) and heat index (°C) at the time
and location of injury were determined using valid online database tools. Acute concussion assessments included the Sport
Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) symptom inventory, Balance Error Scoring System (BESS), and the Immediate Post-
Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT). We used multiple linear regression models to determine whether
heat index and altitude predicted each acute assessment outcome, days-to-asymptomatic, and days-to-return-to-play.
Results Collegiate athletes were concussed at a 181.1 m (range − 0.6 to 2201.9 m) median altitude and 17.8 °C (range − 6.1
to 35.6 °C) median heat index. Altitude did not predict (p ≥ 0.265) any outcomes. Every one-degree increase in heat index
reduced days-to-asymptomatic (p = 0.047; R2 = 0.06) and days-to-return-to-play (p = 0.006; R2 = 0.09) by 0.05 and 0.14 days,
respectively. Heat index and altitude did not explain significant variance in SCAT, BESS, and ImPACT composite scores
(p’s = 0.20–0.922).
Conclusion Our findings suggest that on-field altitude and heat index at the time of injury do not contribute to clinically
meaningful changes on acute assessments or concussion recovery. On-field altitude and heat index do not appear to signifi-
cantly alter assessment outcomes or clinical recovery, suggesting that environmental factors at altitudes below < 2500 m are
negligible outcomes for researchers and clinicians to consider post-concussion.

{
 "id": "Q61",
 "sourceFile": "The influence of movement tempo on acute neuromuscular, hormonal, and mechanical responses to resistance exercise - A mini review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The PDF title 'The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise: A Mini Review' (J Strength Cond Res, 2020) matches the filename and crossrefTitle, with the same authors; the DOI is the batch externalDoi because the article's own DOI is not printed in the text.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Mini review of isotonic resistance-exercise studies that varied movement tempo (the eccentric, pause, concentric and pause durations of each repetition), identified through keyword searches of seven databases with stated inclusion criteria. The included studies were mostly small acute experiments in resistance-trained or recreationally trained adults, and the review does not pool effect sizes. It reports that slower tempos lower the load and number of repetitions a lifter can complete while increasing time under tension, and that lactate, hormone, EMG, RPE and muscle damage responses are inconsistent across studies.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review gives a narrative synthesis with no pooled estimates or formal quality appraisal, so the strength of each finding is hard to judge. Most included studies were small, single-session, and used different tempo notation, loads and exercises, which limits direct comparison.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read tempo as a proven lever for strength or muscle gain, when the review covers acute single-session responses only and its hormone and lactate findings are inconsistent.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Wilk M, Tufano JJ, Zajac A. The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise: A Mini Review. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020;34(8):2369-2383.",
   "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000003636",
   "abstract": "This mini review examines how movement tempo, the duration of each phase of a repetition, changes the acute responses to resistance exercise. Slower tempos reduce the 1RM, the load that can be used and the number of repetitions performed, while increasing time under tension and affecting cardiovascular and hormonal responses. The authors advise coaches to test maximal strength and repetitions at each tempo used.",
   "tldr": "Slower repetition tempos lower the load and number of repetitions a lifter can complete, and they increase total time under tension. Hormone, lactate and muscle damage responses to tempo are inconsistent, so coaches should test 1RM and maximal reps at the tempos they plan to use.",
   "methods": "Narrative mini review of isotonic resistance-exercise studies in healthy adults, found through keyword searches of Google Scholar, MEDLINE, ADONIS, ERIC, SPORTDiscus, EBSCOhost and PubMed. Included studies were original, peer-reviewed, English-language studies using isotonic exercise. No pooled analysis was performed.",
   "findings": "Slower tempos reduced the maximal number of repetitions at a given load. For example, Headley et al. found that 2/0/2/0 gave 6.4 repetitions against 4.7 for 4/0/2/0 at 75% 1RM, and 1RM was 3.7% lower with the 4/0/2/0 tempo. Total time under tension rose with slower tempos, even when total repetitions fell. Post-exercise blood lactate, testosterone, growth hormone and cortisol responses differed between studies, and several studies found no difference. Only a few studies have examined EMG, RPE, muscle damage or cardiovascular responses to tempo, and their findings were mixed.",
   "limitations": "The review is narrative, with no pooled effect sizes or formal risk-of-bias assessment, so selection and weighting of studies cannot be checked. Most included studies were small acute experiments with different loads, exercises and tempo notation, and few isolated concentric or eccentric duration. The authors note that sex differences in tempo responses have not been studied empirically.",
   "practicalImplications": "Test 1RM and maximal repetitions at each tempo used, because a slower tempo lowers the load and number of repetitions a lifter can manage. Track time under tension alongside repetitions when setting training volume, since slower tempos raise time under tension even when repetitions fall. The authors say tempo changes across sessions or within sets can reduce monotony, but tempo-specific programming is still largely trial and error.",
   "athleteDev": "Treat tempo as a planned variable: a slower eccentric phase increases time under tension and requires lower loads, while a faster or explosive concentric suits power work. The review suggests slower tempos may be more activity-specific for sports that need long periods of constant tension, such as wrestling, but it does not measure sport performance outcomes.",
   "rtp": "The review suggests that a variable or slower tempo may help injured athletes who cannot yet lift heavy loads or move explosively, because each phase can be controlled at lower loads. It includes no return-to-sport outcomes or criteria, so it cannot set return-to-sport readiness or load thresholds."
 }
}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Abstract
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Wilk, M, Tufano, JJ, and Zajac, A. The influence of movement tempo on acute neuromuscular, hormonal, and mechanical
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               responses to resistance exercise—a mini review. J Strength Cond Res 34(8): 2369–2383, 2020—Resistance training studies
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               mainly analyze variables such as the type and order of exercise, intensity, number of sets, number of repetitions, and duration and
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               frequency of rest periods. However, one variable that is often overlooked in resistance training research, as well as in practice, is
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               premeditated movement tempo, which can influence a myriad of mechanical and physiological factors associated with training and
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               adaptation. Specifically, this article provides an overview of the available scientific literature and describes how slower tempos
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               negatively affect the 1-repetition maximum, the possible load to be used, and the number of repetitions performed with a given load,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               while also increasing the total time under tension, which can mediate acute cardiovascular and hormonal responses. As a result,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               coaches should consider testing maximal strength and the maximal number of repetitions that can be performed with each
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               movement tempo that is to be used during training. Otherwise, programming resistance training using various movement tempos is
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               more of a trial-and-error approach, rather than being evidence or practice based. Furthermore, practical applications are provided
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               to show how movement tempo can be adjusted for a variety of case study–type scenarios.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Key Words: repetitions, time under tension, 1RM test, testosterone, cortisol, growth hormone

 "id": "Q62",
 "sourceFile": "The Relationship Between Relative Rest and Team Performance Across Competitive Seasons in the National Football League.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The PDF title 'The Relationship Between Relative Rest and Team Performance Across Competitive Seasons in the National Football League' (J Strength Cond Res, 2025) matches the filename and crossrefTitle; the DOI is the batch externalDoi because the article's own DOI is not printed in the text.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Other",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Archival, observational analysis of 12,290 NFL regular-season games from 1970-71 to 2022-23, with each franchise-season treated as a team (1,569 team-seasons). The relative rest index (the difference in days since each team's previous game, compared with its opponent) had a trivial negative correlation with win/loss ratio (r = -0.064, P = 0.011, R2 = 0.004), and win/loss ratio did not differ across eight RRI categories (P = 0.233). Teams that did not make the playoffs had higher average RRI than teams that lost in the divisional round (P = 0.001) or won the Super Bowl (P = 0.040).",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is team-level archival data with no player, injury, training load or recovery measures, so it cannot show how rest affects individual athletes. The authors note confounders such as team skill, injuries and recovery practices, and say a more sensitive analysis is needed.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the null result as proof that rest between games does not matter for players, when the study only measured team win/loss ratio and playoff depth across seasons.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Pinzone AG, Abu-Amara Y, Gant RW, Rivera J, Tagesen EC, Barkley JE, et al. The Relationship Between Relative Rest and Team Performance Across Competitive Seasons in the National Football League. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025.",
   "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000005148",
   "abstract": "This study analyzed all NFL regular-season games from 1970-71 to 2022-23 to test whether relative rest between opponents is related to team win/loss ratio. The relationship was trivial and negative, and win/loss ratio did not differ across rest categories. Teams that went further in the playoffs tended to have less favorable relative rest, and the authors conclude that rest differences have no significant effect on team performance.",
   "tldr": "Across 52 NFL seasons, the rest advantage a team had over its opponent was not linked to win/loss ratio. Teams that went deepest in the playoffs had less favorable rest differences, so schedule rest is unlikely to be a strong driver of team results.",
   "methods": "Regular-season game records were taken from pro-football-reference.com and spot-checked against NFL.com. Relative rest index (RRI) was calculated for each game as the difference in days since each team's previous game, then averaged by team and season. Pearson correlations tested RRI against win/loss ratio, and one-way ANOVAs compared win/loss ratio across eight RRI categories and RRI across six playoff-depth categories.",
   "findings": "Across all 12,290 games, season-average RRI had a trivial negative correlation with win/loss ratio (r = -0.064, P = 0.011, R2 = 0.004). Win/loss ratio did not differ across RRI categories (P = 0.233). RRI differed by playoff depth (P = 0.018, partial eta squared = 0.009): teams that did not make the playoffs had higher RRI than teams that lost in the divisional round (P = 0.001) or won the Super Bowl (P = 0.040).",
   "limitations": "The analysis uses team-level archival records with no player, injury, practice or recovery data, and the authors name team skill, injuries and recovery strategies as possible confounders. The effect sizes are very small (R2 = 0.004 and partial eta squared = 0.009). The abstract says RRI was lower for teams that lost in the Super Bowl and divisional round, while the Results report the Super Bowl winners, and this summary uses the Results. The authors' earlier 2022-season analysis reported a larger positive correlation (r = 0.339), which this study does not replicate.",
   "practicalImplications": "Across 52 NFL seasons, the rest advantage between opponents did not meaningfully change team win/loss ratio, so the league's schedule configuration does not appear to have strong effects on team results. The authors still advise that player recovery from practice and competition should not be underprioritized given the demands of a season.",
   "athleteDev": "Relative rest between opponents should not be used to predict team results or to judge how athletes will perform. The study does not measure individual readiness, so performance staff should manage recovery from practice and games using athlete-level data.",
   "rtp": "The study measures team win/loss ratio and playoff depth, not injury, return to play or individual recovery, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}

15	        Pinzone, AG, Abu-Amara, Y, Gant, RW, Rivera, J, Tagesen, EC, Barkley, JE, and Jajtner, AR. The relationship between relative rest
16	        and team performance across competitive seasons in the national football league. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000,
17	        2025—This investigation aimed to assess the relationship between relative rest index (RRI) and team performance across multiple
18	        seasons of National Football League (NFL) competition. To examine this relationship, all NFL regular season games from the
19	        1970–71 to 2022–23 NFL seasons (N 5 12,290) were analyzed with rest intervals calculated for each team on a game-to-game

      The Relationship Between Relative Rest and Team
      Performance Across Competitive Seasons in the
      National Football League
      Anthony G. Pinzone, Yousuf Abu-Amara, Ryan W. Gant, Jennifer Rivera, Emily C. Tagesen, Jacob E. Barkley,
      and Adam R. Jajtner
      Exercise Science and Exercise Physiology, Kent State University, Kent, Ohio



        Abstract
        Pinzone, AG, Abu-Amara, Y, Gant, RW, Rivera, J, Tagesen, EC, Barkley, JE, and Jajtner, AR. The relationship between relative rest
        and team performance across competitive seasons in the national football league. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000,
        2025—This investigation aimed to assess the relationship between relative rest index (RRI) and team performance across multiple
        seasons of National Football League (NFL) competition. To examine this relationship, all NFL regular season games from the
        1970–71 to 2022–23 NFL seasons (N 5 12,290) were analyzed with rest intervals calculated for each team on a game-to-game
        basis as the number of days between current and previous games. Next, RRI was calculated as the discrepancy in rest intervals
        between competing teams for all games and averaged for all teams across all seasons with teams categorized by season average
        RRI (,20.70; 20.7 to 20.5; 20.5 to 20.25; 20.25 to 0; 0 to 0.25; 0.25 to 0.5; 0.5 to 0.7; .0.70). Win percentage and playoff
        depth (lost in wild card round; lost in divisional round; lost in conference championship; lost in Super Bowl; won Super Bowl; did not
        make playoffs) quantified team performance. Pearson product correlations were implemented to assess the relationship between
        season average RRI and win percentage. One-way analyses of variance assessed differences in win percentage across RRI
        categories and RRI across playoff depth categories. A trivial negative correlation between RRI and win percentage across all
        seasons was noted. Moreover, win percentage did not differ across RRI categories, while RRI was attenuated among teams that
        lost in the Super Bowl and divisional round compared with teams that did not qualify for the playoffs, suggesting that RRI has no
        significant effect on team performance with competitive eras of NFL competition collated.
        Key Words: American football, rest, performance

 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",

 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Repeated-measures, cross-sectional validation study in 14 resistance-trained men (mean age 25.5 years, at least 4 years of training experience) who performed hang clean pulls at seven loads from 20% to 140% of their 1RM hang power clean. A GymAware PowerTool and a Tendo Power Analyzer were attached to the barbell and compared for reliability, bias and agreement. Both devices were reliable for mean barbell velocity (ICC 0.93 to 0.97), and the Tendo overestimated mean and peak barbell velocity by 3.7 to 6.8% and 1.8 to 2.9%, with small between-device effect sizes (MBV g = 0.35 to 0.57; PBV g = 0.23 to 0.54).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The GymAware was used as the criterion device because 3D motion capture was unavailable, and the sample was resistance-trained men only, so results may not transfer to other populations or to women. The authors note that few comparable studies exist for this lift, and that the Tendo's peak velocity reliability fell at heavier loads.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the device agreement as proof that the two velocity devices can be swapped freely, when the authors say they calculate velocity differently and should not be used interchangeably, especially at 140% 1RM.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Kissick CR, Techmanski BS, Comfort P, Suchomel TJ. The Reliability, Bias, Differences, and Agreement Between Velocity Measurement Devices During the Hang Clean Pull. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(3):289-294.",
   "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000005004",
   "abstract": "This study compared the reliability, bias and agreement of two barbell velocity devices (GymAware PowerTool and Tendo Power Analyzer) during the hang clean pull in 14 resistance-trained men across loads from 20% to 140% of 1RM hang power clean. Both devices were reliable, but the Tendo showed proportional bias for mean and peak velocity and fixed bias for peak velocity at 140% 1RM. The authors conclude that the two devices are reliable and that differences between them are not practically meaningful, although the Tendo slightly overestimates velocity.",
   "tldr": "Both velocity devices gave reliable barbell velocity data across hang clean pull loads up to 140% of 1RM. The Tendo overestimated velocity by a small amount and was less reliable for peak velocity at heavier loads, so the two devices should not be used interchangeably.",
   "methods": "Fourteen resistance-trained men completed a 1RM hang power clean test and then hang clean pulls at 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120 and 140% of 1RM, with a GymAware PowerTool and a Tendo Power Analyzer attached to the barbell. Test-retest ICCs and typical error (CV%) were calculated for each device, and least-products regression, with Hedges' g effect sizes, was used to assess bias and differences between devices.",
   "findings": "The GymAware showed excellent reliability for all mean (ICC 0.94 to 0.97) and peak (ICC 0.88 to 0.95) barbell velocity measures. The Tendo was excellent for mean velocity at all loads and for peak velocity at 20 to 80% 1RM, good at 100 and 120%, and moderate at 140%. The Tendo overestimated mean velocity by 3.7 to 6.8% and peak velocity by 1.8 to 2.9%, and it showed proportional bias for both measures and fixed bias for peak velocity at 140% 1RM. Between-device effect sizes were small (MBV g = 0.35 to 0.57; PBV g = 0.23 to 0.54) and were not classed as practically meaningful.",
   "limitations": "The GymAware was used as the criterion device, not 3D motion capture, so the accuracy of both devices against a gold standard is not established. The sample was 14 resistance-trained men, and the authors say results may not generalize to other populations. Comparable hang clean pull data are limited, and the Tendo's peak velocity reliability declined at heavier loads.",
   "practicalImplications": "Either device can give reliable mean and peak barbell velocity during hang clean pulls at loads from 20% to 140% of 1RM hang power clean. The Tendo may become less reliable at heavier loads because it does not correct for horizontal bar movement, so practitioners should read its heavy-load peak velocity values with caution. The authors say the Tendo's small overestimation can be accounted for if the same device is used consistently.",
   "athleteDev": "Coaches using velocity to load hang clean pulls can use either device for monitoring at up to 140% of 1RM hang power clean, but should use one device consistently so that values can be compared over time. Peak velocity from the Tendo at heavy loads should be interpreted with caution.",
   "rtp": "The study tested resistance-trained men in a lab and included no injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or criteria."
 }

      The Reliability, Bias, Differences, and Agreement
      Between Velocity Measurement Devices During the
      Hang Clean Pull
      Cameron R. Kissick,1,2 Baylee S. Techmanski,2,3 Paul Comfort,4,5 and Timothy J. Suchomel2,4,6
      1
       New York Mets, Queens, New York; 2Department of Human Movement Sciences, Carroll University, Waukesha, Wisconsin; 3Athlete
      Performance, Mequon, Wisconsin; 4Directorate of Psychology and Sport, University of Salford, Salford, Greater Manchester, United
      Kingdom; 5Strength and Power Research Group, School of Medical and Health Sciences, Edith Cowan University, Joondalup,
      Western Australia, Australia; and 6Department of Sports Medicine and Nutrition, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania



          Abstract
          Kissick, CR, Techmanski, BS, Comfort, P, and Suchomel, TJ. The reliability, bias, differences, and agreement between velocity
          measurement devices during the hang clean pull. J Strength Cond Res 39(3): 289–294, 2025—This study examined the reliability,
          bias, differences, and agreement between the GymAware PowerTool (GA) and Tendo Power Analyzer (TENDO) during the hang
          clean pull (HCP). Fourteen resistance-trained men performed HCP repetitions with 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, and 140% of their 1
          repetition maximum hang power clean (1RM HPC) with GA and TENDO devices attached to the barbell. Least-products regression
          was used to examine instances of proportional and fixed bias for mean barbell velocity (MBV) and peak barbell velocity (PBV)
          between devices. In addition, Hedge’s g effect sizes were calculated to determine the magnitude of the differences between
          devices. Excellent reliability was displayed by the GA for all measurements. While excellent reliability for the TENDO was displayed
          for MBV across all loads, only moderate-good reliability was present for PBV at loads .80% 1RM. The TENDO displayed
          proportional bias for both MBV and PBV as well as fixed bias for PBV at 140% 1RM compared with the GA. Despite the small effect
          sizes that existed between devices for both MBV (g 5 0.35–0.57) and PBV (g 5 0.23–0.54), none of these differences were
          practically meaningful. The GA and TENDO are reliable devices that can measure MBV and PBV accurately during the HCP;
          however, practitioners should note that the TENDO may overestimate MBV and PBV to a small extent (3.7–6.8% and 1.8–2.9%).
          Key Words: weightlifting, Olympic lift, power clean, velocity-based training, load-velocity profile

 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The PDF title 'The Role of Speed, Change of Direction, and Momentum by Position and Starting Status in Division 1 Collegiate Football Players' (J Strength Cond Res, 2025, Mann, Cowley, Weakley) matches the filename and crossrefTitle; the DOI is the batch externalDoi because the article's own DOI is not printed in the text.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective analysis of 15 years of data from 496 first-year NCAA Division 1 football players from one program (big positions n = 122, mid n = 178, skill n = 196), who completed the 40-yard sprint, pro-agility and L drill tests, with momentum calculated from body mass and average velocity. Positional differences were moderate to very large, and starters were faster and had greater momentum than nonstarters with small to moderate effects (for example, 40-yard sprint of 5.18 vs 5.30 s in big positions). ROC cutoffs to separate starters from nonstarters had AUC values of 0.57 to 0.76 (poor to fair) and positive predictive values of 15% to 43%.",
 "screeningLimitations": "All data came from one program under a single head coach, and starter status was the only selection outcome, so the results may reflect that program's style of play and selection decisions. The ROC thresholds discriminated poorly, and the study tested athletes after a 6-week winter program, not at other times of the year.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could use the ROC cutoffs as a way to pick or cut players, when the authors found the thresholds had poor to fair discrimination and low positive predictive value, and they advise against using them for selection.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Mann JB, Cowley N, Weakley J. The Role of Speed, Change of Direction, and Momentum by Position and Starting Status in Division 1 Collegiate Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(1):41-47.",
   "doi": "10.1519/jsc.0000000000004944",
   "abstract": "This study analyzed 15 years of 40-yard sprint, pro-agility and L drill data from 496 Division 1 football players to compare positional groups and starters with nonstarters. Positions differed in speed and momentum, and starters were faster and had greater momentum than nonstarters. The authors found no practically useful ROC thresholds for separating starters from nonstarters, and they advise against binary selection thresholds.",
   "tldr": "In Division 1 football, positional groups differed in sprint, change of direction and momentum, and starters outperformed nonstarters by small to moderate margins. Cutoffs built from these tests were poor at identifying starters, so the tests should guide development and profiling, not selection.",
   "methods": "Retrospective analysis of performance data from 496 first-year NCAA Division 1 football athletes across 15 years. Athletes were grouped as big, mid or skill position and as starter or nonstarter. Each athlete completed the 40-yard sprint, pro-agility and L drill, with momentum calculated from body mass and average velocity. Linear mixed models compared groups, and ROC curves set cutoffs for starter status.",
   "findings": "Positional groups differed significantly on all tests, with moderate to very large effects. Starters were faster than nonstarters within each positional group (for example, 40-yard sprint 5.18 vs 5.30 s in big positions, 4.70 vs 4.87 s in mid, and 4.52 vs 4.69 s in skill), with small to moderate effects, and had greater momentum. ROC curves gave AUC values of 0.57 to 0.76 (poor to fair), with sensitivity up to 94% but positive predictive values of 15% to 43%.",
   "limitations": "The data come from a single program under one head coach, so playing style and selection practices may have shaped the results. Starter status was the only outcome, and binary ROC models had poor to fair discrimination. The authors suggest that multivariable methods and larger datasets would be needed to build better selection tools.",
   "practicalImplications": "Coaches should profile positions using different measures: emphasize absolute sprint and change of direction time for skill players, and monitor momentum for big players. The authors advise against using these tests with fixed thresholds to select or cut players, since the ROC cutoffs had low positive predictive value. Speed, change of direction and momentum should be developed alongside technical and tactical ability.",
   "athleteDev": "Use the position profile to set development priorities: skill players should build absolute speed and change of direction, big players need enough body mass to create momentum, and mid players should balance both. The paper advises developing these qualities rather than using them as a selection tool.",
   "rtp": "The study does not include injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, and it offers no return-to-play thresholds. The tests describe general performance by position, so they cannot be used to decide whether an athlete is ready to return to sport."
 }
}

                                                                                                           Abstract
                                                                                                           Mann, JB, Cowley, N, and Weakley, J. The role of speed, change of direction, and momentum by position and starting status in
                                                                                                           Division 1 collegiate football players. J Strength Cond Res 39(1): 41–47, 2025—This study (a) investigated differences between big,
                                                                                                           mid, and skill positions in sprint and change of direction times and momentum; (b) compared starting and nonstarting athletes; and
                                                                                                           (c) investigated whether thresholds can be developed to distinguish between starting and nonstarting Division 1 collegiate football
                                                                                                           athletes. Data from 496 collegiate football players who completed the 40-yard dash, pro-agility, and L drill were analyzed. Mo-
                                                                                                           mentum was calculated using body mass and the average velocity during each test. To assess differences between positions and
                                                                                                           starters and nonstarters, data were analyzed using linear mixed models with effect size 695% confidence intervals. Receiver




        CX1AWnYQp/IlQrHD3i3D0OdRyi7TvSFl4Cf3VC4/OAVpDDa8KKGKV0Ymy+78= on 12/10/2024
                                                                                                           operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated to determine whether a cutoff value could be used to distinguish starters from
                                                                                                           nonstarters. Significant differences for both time and momentum were found between positional groups and starters and non-
                                                                                                           starters for all tests in all positions. Starting skill position players tended to have greater differences in sprint or change of direction
                                                                                                           times and starting big players had greater sprint momentum. However, it should be noted that all ROC curves demonstrated
                                                                                                           relatively poor predictive value. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that bigger, faster players are preferentially selected in
                                                                                                           collegiate Division 1 football and there may be value in coaches collecting and assessing different outcome measures (e.g., sprint
                                                                                                           times and sprint momentum) depending on the positional group of the player. Finally, it should be acknowledged that setting binary
                                                                                                           thresholds to guide selection decisions is ill-advised and that speed, change of direction, and momentum are only one piece of the
                                                                                                           performance puzzle.
                                                                                                           Key Words: American football, performance, team sports, sprinting, testing, strength and conditioning

import json, os, sys
BASE = sys.argv[1]
def load(i):
    return json.load(open(os.path.join(BASE, 'drafts', i + '.json')))
def save(i, r):
    with open(os.path.join(BASE, 'verified', i + '.json'), 'w') as f:
        json.dump(r, f, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.write('\n')
def rep(s, old, new):
    assert old in s, (old[:60])
    return s.replace(old, new)

# Q57
r = load('Q57')
r['evidenceSummary'] = rep(r['evidenceSummary'],
    "with 272 participants who were 88% male and healthy, trained or recreationally active.",
    "with 272 healthy participants who were highly trained or recreationally active; 22 of the 25 studies (88%) tested males only.")
r['verification'] = {"status": "CORRECTED", "changes": [
    "evidenceSummary: '272 participants who were 88% male' misread the study-level split -> 88% of studies used all-male samples ('males 88%; both males and females 12%' refers to the 25 studies)"],
    "residualConcerns": "", "spotCheckPriority": "normal"}
save('Q57', r)

# Q58
r = load('Q58')
r['evidenceSummary'] = ("Repeated-measures laboratory study of 25 healthy volunteers (10 women, 15 men; mean age 24.8 years) performing drop jump, running and 180 degree change-of-direction movements barefoot, with fresh ankle tape, and after 15 minutes of sports-specific use; only the barefoot and fresh-tape order was randomized. "
    "Fresh tape significantly reduced peak ankle inversion (change of direction: 15.4 vs 11.3 degrees barefoot vs fresh; drop jump: 12.3 vs 9.1 degrees), and used tape still reduced it. "
    "Fresh tape significantly increased the peak loading rate of the resultant ground reaction force in all three movements (for example, change of direction 544.5 vs 643.5 N/kg/s), and most knee and hip risk-factor variables were unchanged.")
r['paper']['tldr'] = ("Ankle tape reduced peak ankle inversion in drop jumps and change-of-direction movements, and the effect was still present after 15 minutes of use. "
    "The tape also increased the loading rate of ground reaction force in all three movements, which may raise overuse risk, although the practical significance of this is unclear.")
r['paper']['methods'] = ("Twenty-five healthy participants (10 women, 15 men) completed drop jumps (25 cm), running (4.5 m/s), and 180 degree change-of-direction tasks barefoot under three conditions: no tape, fresh standard ankle taping, and taping after 15 minutes of sports-specific activity. "
    "Barefoot and fresh-tape conditions were randomized in order, and the used-tape condition always came last. "

All eight records are written to `verified/` and every decision stays INCLUDE. Seven needed corrections and only Q59 passed unchanged. Q60 uses the article DOI printed in the PDF, not the external one.

- **Q57**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED. The draft said the 272 participants were 88% male. The 88% is actually the share of studies (22 of 25) that tested only males.
- **Q58**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high priority. The draft said tape reduced ankle inversion during running, but inversion was only measured in drop jumps and cutting. The draft also missed that tape raised the loading rate in the drop jump. It called the design randomized, but only the order of the no-tape and fresh-tape conditions was randomized. The text and tables disagree on some statistics, which I noted.
- **Q59**: INCLUDE, VERIFIED, high priority only because it covers heart and lung risks (arrhythmia, vaping lung injury). No errors found.
- **Q60**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED, high priority. The external DOI belongs to the separate "Correction to:" notice (2021), so the record uses the DOI printed on page 1, 10.1007/s40279-020-01395-5. This goes against the batch rule to use the external DOI, so the operator should confirm it. Number fixes:
  - The heat index p-value for clinical recovery is 0.010 in the table; the 0.006 the draft used is the whole model's p-value.
  - Only male sex predicted recovery; concussion history did not.
  - The draft flagged a conflict that wasn't one (0.22 and 7.12 days come from the away-games model). The real conflict is between the abstract and the table.
  - Heat index was significant for ImPACT reaction time (p = 0.039), though that model as a whole was not significant.
  - The PDF year is 2020; Crossref lists 2021 for the correction notice.
- **Q61**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED. The methods field called it a narrative review, which conflicted with its systematic-review coding; the paper does describe a database search. Fixed the summary of the blood pressure and muscle damage findings, and noted that some advice rests on the authors' unpublished data.
- **Q62**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED. "Teams that went deepest in the playoffs had less rest" overstated it: only teams that lost in the divisional round or won the Super Bowl differed from non-playoff teams. Removed advice about athlete recovery that the study doesn't test.
- **Q63**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED. The Tendo's bias appeared only at 140% of 1RM, not at all loads. Reliability was measured across repeat lifts in one session, not test-retest. Added a conflict between the text and table on one reliability value, and changed the population tag to Adult / Recreational.
- **Q64**: INCLUDE, CORRECTED (minor). Added limitations: two tests were hand-timed, testing was in the first year while starter status counted any start across the career, and one AUC is labelled "fair" when the paper's own cut-offs make it "poor". Attributed the position-by-position advice to the authors.
